A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ThinkEdit, with matching core methods and benchmarks. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and relocated or reformatted content can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original steering, attention-head analysis and weight-editing experiments, including benchmark results in Tables 1–3 and appendix case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds editing-rate comparisons, an evaluated continuation baseline, overall reasoning-length measurements and 32B model results.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the default intervention from editing the top 2% to the top 4% of attention heads. Direction extraction, head scoring and orthogonal weight projection remain the same; this is a limited change to intervention scope.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K training data and evaluate GSM8K, MMLU Elementary Math, MATH-Level1, MATH-Level5 and MATH-500. The additional model sizes and editing configurations retain this mathematical task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates ThinkEdit against unmodified models and discusses appending "Wait" only conceptually. v3 adds an evaluated "Append Wait" comparator across the benchmarks in Appendices A.4–A.5, introducing a substantive alternative to weight editing.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 reports collecting 2,000 GSM8K responses instead of 1,000. v3 also introduces a 2%/4%/8% editing-rate comparison, continuation triggered below 500 tokens, and evaluation of a 32B model. The retained benchmark sizes and generation caps are unchanged; the revised calibration description does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices A.3–A.4 add editing-rate sensitivity and analyses comparing accuracy, shortest-response lengths and overall reasoning lengths against simple continuation. These examine intervention strength and token-use tradeoffs absent from v1's fixed-rate evaluation. Earlier steering analyses and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 independent runs and report accuracy with mean and ± values. Added tables extend the existing reporting format, without a documented change in run counts, seed policy, uncertainty estimation or statistical testing.

E6.justification: v1's 2% results are retained unchanged in v3 Tables 5, 7 and 8. The main tables now present newly reported 4% results: for example, 1.5B MMLU Elementary Math accuracy is 90.66%, while the retained 2% result is 86.24%. Additional 8%, "Wait", overall-length and 32B entries substantially expand the findings, including mixed 32B outcomes on MATH.

T1.justification: The reasoning-direction definitions, attention-head contribution formulas and projection update remain mathematically equivalent. v3 consolidates the embedding-average notation and corrects an equation reference in the overview figure, without adding or revising theoretical reasoning or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims about reasoning-length directions and targeted head editing remain. The abstract, contributions and conclusion revise the claimed tradeoff from 2% of heads and 0.1% of parameters to 4% and 0.2%, with reported short-reasoning/overall gains changing from +5.44%/+2.43% to +6.39%/+3.34%.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of selective lengthening with little aggregate length change, dataset-dependent editing-rate tradeoffs, and the comparison with "Wait". Appendix A.5 discusses limited overall gains for 32B on MATH, while the new Limitations section qualifies applicability to models already producing sufficiently long reasoning.

D1.justification: v3 revises the documented calibration sample count and default editing percentage, and specifies the new baseline's 500-token trigger. Code access, A100 hardware disclosure, CoT-tag processing and generation caps remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 removes the Llama 3 report by Dubey et al. and the Qwen2.5-1M report by Yang et al., alongside their architecture-background passage. The remaining cited works and positioning within representation engineering and attention-head intervention are substantially retained.

P1.justification: Most introduction and method prose is retained. v3 shortens background, related-work and conclusion passages, consolidates notation, reorganizes appendix discussions and adds a separate Limitations section. These are limited editorial changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text to two columns, regroups steering panels between the main text and appendix, relocates the shortest-length table and adds Tables 4–12. It also highlights short-length regions, simplifies heatmap ticks and reformats case-study panels; the two steering examples exchange order.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical validation by addressing v1's lack of an evaluated continuation alternative, editing-rate sensitivity and overall reasoning-length accounting. The 32B results and explicit applicability limitation also clarify where benefits weaken. Some new interpretations overgeneralize: Tables 5 and 7 contain "Wait" wins, and Table 4's aggregate length change masks sizable dataset-specific increases. Despite these weaknesses, the added evidence materially improves assessment of the intervention's benefits and limits.
